extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, scholarly-communication professionals, and researchers interested in peer review and the future of academic publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive criteria for moving scholarly journal peer review from a human-dependent system toward a predominantly AI-based system, including intermediate hybrid models and social/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional recognition of peer-review service
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether universities and research institutions consider voluntary peer-review service in appointment, promotion, tenure, or annual evaluation decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that only some universities (e.g., Technical University of Munich, University of Warwick, University of Pittsburgh) explicitly consider reviewing; lack of broad institutional recognition undermines peer-review as an academic responsibility and reduces reviewer motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer motivation: access to latest research as incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is sometimes motivated by the opportunity to learn about the latest research prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article questions whether access to millions of preprints and other open materials already suffices for this motivation, implying that reviewer incentives should be assessed relative to available alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity and sustainability of 'good karma' motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on reciprocity (review one another) and 'good karma' as a sustainable incentive model for securing reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, recently-published authors often decline review requests; the simple logic that each author will perform at least one review per paper is not reliably sustained, undermining system sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity limits in grant and proposal review
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocity logic does not apply uniformly across different review types, such as research project proposal review, where reviewers often cannot be applicants themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal experience cited where long volunteer engagement without reciprocation led to disengagement—indicating differing incentive structures across review domains must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and acknowledgement of co-reviewers / prevention of ghost-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing 'peer review ghost-writing' and the practice of unacknowledged co-review contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-reviewer concepts can provide proper credit but may also be used to expand voluntary reviewer pools; systems should ensure appropriate acknowledgement to avoid exploitation and hidden labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer burden, time cost, and recognition mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The aggregate time and monetary value of peer review labor and the need for meaningful recognition for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2020 reviewers spent ~130 million hours; recognition services (Clarivate Web of Science Reviewer Recognition Service, IOP Trusted Reviewer Certification, Frontiers’ name disclosure) exist but often lack tangible material benefits—systems should consider concrete incentives or compensation models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and the Global North–Global South divide
rubrics_metrics.description: How peer review practices and related costs (e.g., APCs) reinforce geographical and economic inequities in scholarly publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paid review models risk adding undue burden and worsening the divide; reforms should be evaluated for their distributional effects across regions and incomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial fairness relative to publisher profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the current model (unpaid reviewer labor supporting highly profitable publishers) is economically fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post highlights large publisher profit margins and the $10-billion journal publishing industry's reliance on unpaid labor, arguing this imbalance should inform choices about compensating reviewers or adopting AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI limitations: lack of human critical thinking and bias risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that AI cannot perform human-like critical thinking, and that algorithmic biases will persist or be entrenched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues for careful training of AI to reduce algorithmic limitations; opponents in comments warn AI could disguise or cement existing biases if deployed prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of AI tools' effectiveness and readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical/observational assessment of current AI-run article review software and models for effectiveness and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing reviews show some degrees of effectiveness and efficiency, but generally that tools are not yet ready to fully replace human reviewers; deployment should be phased and evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial AI screening / triage criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks appropriate for early AI adoption: efficient initial quality checks and potential desk rejection based on objective checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI should assess whether a submission matches journal scope and check overall structure, plagiarism level, language, coherence among sections, and basics of research ethics, integrity, transparency, and reproducibility. Note many tools check these elements separately—integrated solutions are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of separate automated checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to combine multiple specialized tools (plagiarism, language, structure, ethics checks) into cohesive AI-based screening workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post observes that many tools already exist but operate individually; successful AI triage requires integration to make reliable initial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI assessment of human review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Training AI to evaluate the quality of human reviewers' reports and to add complementary notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some models already attempt this with variable consistency and accuracy; such tools could improve review quality management and meta-review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid review model: AI as one reviewer with human oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Using AI as one reviewer among human reviewers, with authors responding to both kinds of reviews and editors making decisions based on combined input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this model at least one human reviewer should check revised manuscripts; tools like ResearchAdvisor exist but show limitations—human oversight remains essential during hybrid phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully AI-based review with editorial final reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal phase where AI is the sole reviewer, authors respond to AI comments, and editors perform a final reading before decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires a 'huge technological leap' and robust trust in AI's abilities; editors still play a decisive role initially in final reading and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased transition roadmap for adopting AI in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-phase sequence from 100% human-dependent review to a completely AI-based system, each phase defining roles for AI, humans, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phases: (1) no AI; (2) AI-assisted triage producing desk rejections and checks, then human review; (3) AI assessing review reports and adding notes; (4) AI as one reviewer alongside humans; (5) AI as sole reviewer with editors finalizing. The author suggests pooled publisher efforts to manage a rationally-paced long-term transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural readiness for technological scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing diverse socio-cultural-political human systems to adopt AI tools in publishing so adoption is equitable and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that focusing on technological innovations without preparing human systems (norms, training, expectations) risks inequitable or ineffective rollout; publishers and associations should allocate time and resources to support stakeholders' preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of AI hallucinations and fabricated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: AI's tendency to invent or misattribute citations and sources, undermining trust in its bibliographic assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted AI may make up citations (legal-case controversy referenced) so AI cannot currently be trusted to reliably validate a submission's bibliography or detect fabricated sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of paying reviewers vs technological replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether addressing unpaid reviewer labor via compensation is preferable to replacing reviewers with AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argue paying reviewers (or otherwise materially compensating them) could be an easier, fairer route than attempting a full technological replacement; trade-offs include bureaucracy, costs, conflicts of interest, and equity implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of human expertise in judging substantive quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of domain experts to judge the substantive and conceptual quality of manuscripts, not just editorial or technical checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several comments emphasize that while AI can help with grammar, plagiarism, and fakery checks, evaluating the paper's scientific or scholarly merit requires human experts for the foreseeable future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding quality over quantity of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting incentives in academia to value the quality of outputs rather than the number of publications as a way to address core problems in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recommend reorienting evaluation systems (hiring, promotion, funding) to reward quality to reduce publish-or-perish pressures that drive poor review practices and exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on post-publication verification and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing on objective, active confirmation of findings (replication/validation) rather than relying solely on pre-publication peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters argue that with high rates of irreproducible results, systems should move toward active confirmation of claims as a better quality-control mechanism than traditional (human or AI) peer review alone.
